title: Building blocks
intro: The vocabulary of distributed systems, each in four lines: what it is, how it works, when to reach for it, and the way it bites. These are the words you need to use precisely in an interview. Each links to the lessons where it appears.

blocks.name: CAP and PACELC
blocks.what: CAP: during a network partition, a distributed store must choose availability or consistency. PACELC adds: even without a partition, you trade latency for consistency on every operation.
blocks.how: A partition-tolerant system either refuses writes it cannot replicate (CP) or accepts them and reconciles later (AP). Synchronous replication is the latency cost of consistency in normal operation.
blocks.reachFor: Use PACELC to explain why you chose async replication (latency) or quorum writes (consistency) for a specific dataset.
blocks.gotcha: 'We chose AP' is meaningless without saying what conflict resolution looks like and what the user sees during the inconsistency window.

blocks.name: Linearizability and the consistency spectrum
blocks.what: Linearizable: every operation appears to happen atomically at some instant between its start and end, system-wide. Below it: sequential, causal, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, eventual.
blocks.how: Linearizability needs a single order agreed by all replicas, usually via consensus or a single leader with synchronous replication. Weaker models drop global ordering for speed.
blocks.reachFor: Name the exact model each operation needs. Ledgers need linearizable; comment threads need causal; like counts need eventual.
blocks.gotcha: Serializability (transactions) and linearizability (single operations) are different; strict serializability is both. Spanner gives you that at the cost of commit latency.

blocks.name: Consensus (Raft, Paxos)
blocks.what: A protocol by which a set of nodes agree on a sequence of values despite crashes, used for leader election, configuration, and replicated logs.
blocks.how: Raft elects a leader by majority vote with terms; the leader appends entries to its log and commits them once a majority acknowledges. A minority partition cannot elect a leader, which prevents split-brain.
blocks.reachFor: Anywhere two nodes must never both believe they are in charge: database failover, lock services, shard map ownership, etcd and ZooKeeper.
blocks.gotcha: Consensus needs a majority alive: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. Two-node clusters cannot do consensus. Consensus is slow (round trips) so keep it off the hot path.

blocks.name: Quorum reads and writes
blocks.what: With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgments and a read consults R replicas. If W plus R exceeds N, reads overlap the latest write.
blocks.how: Tunable per operation in Cassandra and Dynamo-style stores: ONE, QUORUM, ALL. Read repair and anti-entropy fix stale replicas in the background.
blocks.reachFor: When one table needs both fast eventual reads and occasional strongly consistent reads, without changing the database.
blocks.gotcha: Quorum gives you consistency, not isolation: concurrent writes still need conflict resolution (last-writer-wins, vector clocks, or CRDTs).

blocks.name: Two-phase commit and sagas
blocks.what: 2PC: a coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then tells them all to commit. Sagas: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions to undo earlier steps on failure.
blocks.how: 2PC blocks participants while waiting for the coordinator; a coordinator crash leaves them stuck. Sagas never block: each step commits locally and failures run compensations in reverse.
blocks.reachFor: Sagas for cross-service workflows (order, payment, inventory). 2PC only inside a single database system or where blocking is acceptable.
blocks.gotcha: Sagas lack isolation: intermediate states are visible. Design compensations to be idempotent and expect to reconcile when a compensation itself fails.

blocks.name: Idempotency
blocks.what: An operation that produces the same result whether applied once or many times.
blocks.how: Clients attach a unique key per logical operation; the server records the key with the outcome and returns the recorded outcome on repeats. Consumers of queues deduplicate by message id.
blocks.reachFor: Every mutating API and every queue consumer, because networks fail after commit and before acknowledgment, so retries are unavoidable.
blocks.gotcha: Idempotency keys need a TTL and a scope (per user, per endpoint). Natural idempotency (set x = 5) is better than key tables when the operation allows it.

blocks.name: Clocks, Lamport timestamps, and vector clocks
blocks.what: Wall clocks drift and cannot order events across machines. Logical clocks order events by causality instead.
blocks.how: A Lamport timestamp is a counter incremented on each event and bumped to the max on receive, giving a total order consistent with causality. Vector clocks keep one counter per node and detect concurrency.
blocks.reachFor: Ordering events in a distributed log, detecting conflicting concurrent writes, versioning in multi-leader replication.
blocks.gotcha: Never use wall-clock timestamps for last-writer-wins across machines unless you have Spanner-style bounded clocks. Vector clocks grow with node count.

blocks.name: Leases and distributed locks
blocks.what: A lease is a lock with an expiry, granted by a coordination service, that must be renewed to remain held.
blocks.how: A node acquires the lease via consensus (etcd, ZooKeeper) and renews it periodically. If it stops renewing, the lease expires and another node can take over. Fencing tokens prevent a paused old holder from acting after expiry.
blocks.reachFor: Single-writer guarantees: one scheduler running cron, one primary accepting writes, one worker processing a partition.
blocks.gotcha: A client can be paused (GC, network) past its lease and still think it holds the lock. Always pass a fencing token to the resource so stale holders are rejected.

blocks.name: Consistent hashing
blocks.what: A way to map keys to nodes so that adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.
blocks.how: Nodes and keys are hashed onto a ring; each key belongs to the next node clockwise. Virtual nodes (many points per physical node) smooth the distribution.
blocks.reachFor: Distributed caches, sharded stores, and any time you rebalance across a changing fleet.
blocks.gotcha: It balances key count, not load; a hot key still overloads one node. Pair with replication of hot keys or request-level load awareness.

blocks.name: Partitioning strategies
blocks.what: Range, hash, and composite partitioning decide which node owns which keys and what queries stay local.
blocks.how: Range keeps adjacent keys together (good scans, hot ranges). Hash spreads keys (even load, no scans). Composite prefixes a high-cardinality key with a secondary dimension to get both.
blocks.reachFor: Choose by the dominant query: range for time windows per entity, hash for point lookups, composite for time series per device.
blocks.gotcha: Monotonic keys under range partitioning send all writes to one partition. Low-cardinality keys cannot spread load no matter how you hash them.

blocks.name: Replication models
blocks.what: Single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless replication, each with sync or async propagation.
blocks.how: Single-leader is simple and consistent with failover risk. Multi-leader accepts writes in several places and must resolve conflicts. Leaderless (Dynamo) uses quorums and repair.
blocks.reachFor: Single-leader by default. Multi-leader only for geo-distributed writes with a conflict strategy. Leaderless for availability-first key-value workloads.
blocks.gotcha: Async replication means failover loses the last unreplicated writes; measure lag and decide what RPO you are promising.

blocks.name: Change data capture
blocks.what: Reading a database's write-ahead or binlog and emitting every committed change as an ordered event stream.
blocks.how: A connector (Debezium) tails the log and publishes to Kafka; consumers build caches, search indexes, warehouses, or migrate to a new store from the stream.
blocks.reachFor: Keeping derived stores in sync without dual-write code; datastore migrations; event streams from a system that was not built to emit events.
blocks.gotcha: CDC lags; consumers must be idempotent and tolerate reordering across tables. Schema changes in the source must be handled in the stream.

blocks.name: Transactional outbox
blocks.what: Writing the event you want to publish into a table in the same transaction as the business change, then publishing from that table.
blocks.how: A relay polls or tails the outbox table and publishes to the broker, marking rows sent. Consumers deduplicate because the relay may publish twice.
blocks.reachFor: Any time a service must both update its database and tell others, to avoid the dual-write race.
blocks.gotcha: The relay is at-least-once; the outbox table needs cleanup; ordering is per-aggregate, not global.

blocks.name: Event sourcing and CQRS
blocks.what: Storing state as an append-only log of events and deriving current state by replay; CQRS separates the write model from read models built from the events.
blocks.how: Commands append events; projections consume them to build query-optimized views. Snapshots bound replay time.
blocks.reachFor: Audit-heavy domains, temporal queries, and systems where many read models are derived from one source of truth.
blocks.gotcha: Event schemas are forever; migrations of old events are painful. Projections lag, so reads are eventually consistent. Most systems need a slice of this, not all of it.

blocks.name: B-trees versus LSM trees
blocks.what: B-trees update pages in place and are read-optimized. LSM trees buffer writes in memory, flush sorted runs, and compact in the background, favoring writes.
blocks.how: B-trees give predictable reads and in-place updates with random I/O on writes. LSM gives sequential writes and high ingest rates with read amplification and compaction cost.
blocks.reachFor: B-tree (Postgres, MySQL) for mixed OLTP. LSM (Cassandra, RocksDB, ClickHouse) for write-heavy and time series.
blocks.gotcha: LSM compaction can stall writes and spike latency; tombstones make deletes expensive. B-trees fragment and need vacuum or rebuilds.

blocks.name: Inverted index
blocks.what: A map from each term to the documents that contain it, with positions and weights.
blocks.how: Documents are tokenized and analyzed; the index stores postings lists per term; queries intersect and score postings (BM25) for relevance.
blocks.reachFor: Full-text search, faceting, autocomplete, and relevance ranking that B-trees cannot do.
blocks.gotcha: Indexing is write-heavy and should be async; mapping changes require a reindex; too many shards exhaust the cluster.

blocks.name: Bloom filter
blocks.what: A probabilistic set that answers 'definitely not present' or 'possibly present' in constant time with tiny memory.
blocks.how: K hash functions set bits in a bit array on insert; a lookup checks all K bits. False positives are possible, false negatives are not.
blocks.reachFor: Avoiding disk reads for keys that do not exist (LSM SSTables), deduplicating seen URLs in a crawler, checking username availability cheaply.
blocks.gotcha: You cannot delete from a standard Bloom filter; size it for the expected count or the false positive rate climbs.

blocks.name: Columnar storage
blocks.what: Storing each column contiguously instead of each row, so scans read only the columns they need and compress far better.
blocks.how: Parquet files and column stores (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake) read a handful of columns across billions of rows, with vectorized execution.
blocks.reachFor: Analytics, aggregations, and any query that touches few columns of many rows.
blocks.gotcha: Point updates and single-row reads are slow; columnar stores are for append and scan, not OLTP.

blocks.name: Time-series storage
blocks.what: Stores optimized for timestamped values with high ingest, downsampling, retention, and range queries.
blocks.how: Partition by time and series, compress deltas, pre-aggregate rollups at several resolutions, and tier old data to cheaper storage.
blocks.reachFor: Metrics, telemetry, IoT, and financial ticks.
blocks.gotcha: Cardinality (number of distinct series) is the scaling limit, not points per second. One unbounded label can take the store down.

blocks.name: Timeouts, retries, and backoff
blocks.what: A timeout bounds how long a caller waits; retries recover from transient failures; exponential backoff with jitter keeps retries from synchronizing.
blocks.how: Set timeouts below the caller's remaining budget; retry only idempotent operations; cap retries and spend from a retry budget; add random jitter.
blocks.reachFor: Every network call, configured deliberately rather than inherited from a library default.
blocks.gotcha: Retries at every layer multiply (3 at the client times 3 at the gateway times 3 at the service is 27). Retry at one layer and make the rest fail fast.

blocks.name: Circuit breaker
blocks.what: A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency after a threshold and fails fast until a probe succeeds.
blocks.how: Closed, open, half-open states driven by failure rate over a window. Pair with a fallback and scope per dependency.
blocks.reachFor: Any call to a dependency that can be slow, to protect the caller's threads and give the dependency room to recover.
blocks.gotcha: Without a fallback it just makes failures faster. Without a minimum request volume it trips on noise.

blocks.name: Bulkheads
blocks.what: Isolating resources (thread pools, connection pools, queues) per dependency or tenant so one failure cannot consume everything.
blocks.how: Dedicated pools with fixed sizes; when a pool is exhausted, calls to that dependency fail fast while others continue.
blocks.reachFor: Services that call several dependencies, and multi-tenant systems where one tenant's load must not starve others.
blocks.gotcha: Pool sizing is a capacity decision; too small causes false rejections, too large defeats the purpose.

blocks.name: Load shedding and backpressure
blocks.what: Rejecting excess work early and cheaply so the accepted work completes within SLO, and signaling upstream to slow down.
blocks.how: Admission control by queue length or latency; priority tiers so critical requests survive; bounded queues that reject rather than grow; explicit flow control in streams.
blocks.reachFor: Any system that can be overloaded, which is every system, before the overload rather than during.
blocks.gotcha: Shedding must be cheaper than serving; a rejection that does a database lookup is not shedding.

blocks.name: Token bucket and sliding window
blocks.what: Algorithms that bound request rate per key while allowing controlled bursts.
blocks.how: Token bucket refills at a rate and allows bursts up to capacity. Sliding window counters approximate exact windows cheaply. Sliding log is exact but memory heavy.
blocks.reachFor: API protection, fairness between tenants, and cost control on expensive endpoints.
blocks.gotcha: Distributed limiting needs a shared counter or accepts imprecision; return Retry-After or you create a retry storm.

blocks.name: Hedged requests
blocks.what: Sending a second copy of a request to another replica after a short delay and using whichever answers first.
blocks.how: Hedge only after the p95 latency has elapsed so most requests never hedge; cancel the loser.
blocks.reachFor: Cutting tail latency on read paths with replicas, especially fan-out queries.
blocks.gotcha: It adds load (up to 5 percent at the p95 threshold) and must only be used for idempotent reads.

blocks.name: Cache patterns
blocks.what: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind, and refresh-ahead, plus TTL and invalidation strategies.
blocks.how: Cache-aside is application-managed; read-through and write-through put the cache in front of the store; write-behind batches writes; refresh-ahead renews hot keys before expiry.
blocks.reachFor: Cache-aside for most reads; write-through where staleness is unacceptable; write-behind only for loss-tolerant counters.
blocks.gotcha: Stampedes on expiry, stale data after writes, and the cold cache after a restart are the three failures to design for explicitly.

blocks.name: CDN and edge compute
blocks.what: Globally distributed caches and small runtimes close to users that serve content and run logic without reaching the origin.
blocks.how: DNS or anycast routes users to the nearest point of presence; cache keys and TTLs decide hits; edge functions handle auth, routing, and personalization.
blocks.reachFor: Static assets always; cacheable API responses, TLS termination, DDoS absorption, and geo-routing as you scale.
blocks.gotcha: Cache keys that include cookies or query strings defeat caching; invalidation is slow, so version URLs instead.

blocks.name: Unique id generation
blocks.what: Producing globally unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit ids without a central database sequence.
blocks.how: Snowflake: timestamp bits plus worker id bits plus sequence bits. Alternatives: UUIDv7 (time-ordered UUID), database ticket servers, or ranges leased from a coordinator.
blocks.reachFor: Sharded systems where auto-increment is impossible and ids must sort by time for indexes and pagination.
blocks.gotcha: Clock skew can produce duplicates or out-of-order ids; worker ids must be unique, which needs coordination at startup.

blocks.name: Geohash and spatial indexes
blocks.what: Encoding a location as a string whose prefix identifies a grid cell, so nearby points share prefixes.
blocks.how: Interleave latitude and longitude bits; longer strings mean smaller cells. Query a cell and its eight neighbors to find nearby items. Alternatives: S2 cells, quadtrees, R-trees.
blocks.reachFor: Nearby search for drivers, restaurants, or friends; partitioning location data.
blocks.gotcha: Cells at a prefix boundary split neighbors across cells, so always query neighbors; cell sizes vary with latitude.

blocks.name: Fan-out on write versus read
blocks.what: Precomputing each consumer's view when data is produced (write) versus assembling it on request (read).
blocks.how: Write fan-out pushes to every follower's inbox at post time: cheap reads, expensive writes for popular producers. Read fan-out merges sources at request time: cheap writes, expensive reads.
blocks.reachFor: Hybrid: write fan-out for most, read fan-out for the few producers with huge audiences.
blocks.gotcha: Write fan-out for a celebrity is millions of writes per post; read fan-out for a user following thousands is a slow merge. Measure the distribution.

blocks.name: Cursor pagination
blocks.what: Paging by a stable sort key (the last item seen) rather than by offset.
blocks.how: The server returns an opaque cursor encoding the last key; the next request seeks past it with an index. Constant cost per page and stable under inserts.
blocks.reachFor: Every list endpoint from day one.
blocks.gotcha: Cursors must encode the full sort key for ties; jumping to page N is not possible, which is almost always fine.

blocks.name: Feature flags and progressive delivery
blocks.what: Runtime switches that decouple deploying code from exposing behavior, enabling canaries, percentage rollouts, and instant kill switches.
blocks.how: A flag service evaluates rules (percentage, tenant, user) per request; the deploy pipeline ramps exposure while watching SLOs; rollback is a flag flip.
blocks.reachFor: Every risky change, every migration cutover, every experiment.
blocks.gotcha: Flags that never get removed become permanent branches; flag evaluation must be cached and fail safe when the flag service is down.

blocks.name: Distributed tracing
blocks.what: Following one request across services by propagating a trace id and recording timed spans at each hop.
blocks.how: Instrumentation (OpenTelemetry) injects trace context into headers and messages; a collector stores spans; tail-based sampling keeps slow and failed traces.
blocks.reachFor: Any system with more than a couple of services, from day one, because it cannot be added during an incident.
blocks.gotcha: Context must cross queues and async boundaries or traces break exactly where you need them; 100 percent sampling at scale is unaffordable.

blocks.name: Relationship-based authorization
blocks.what: Modeling permissions as relationships (user is editor of doc, doc is in folder, folder is owned by team) and answering 'can X do Y to Z' by graph traversal.
blocks.how: A central service stores relationship tuples and evaluates rules with caching and consistency tokens (Zanzibar, SpiceDB, OpenFGA).
blocks.reachFor: Sharing models, nested resources, and any product where RBAC becomes a tangle of special cases.
blocks.gotcha: The check is on every request, so latency and cache consistency matter; a stale cache can grant revoked access.
